chapters.name: INTRO
chapters.summary: Why a lookup is instant with an index and painfully slow without one.

chapters.name: FULL TABLE SCAN
chapters.summary: Without an index the database reads every row and every page, so cost grows linearly with the table.

chapters.name: SORTED INDEX
chapters.summary: A sorted key-plus-pointer structure enables binary search, but inserts must shift entries and rewrite pages.

chapters.name: BINARY TREES
chapters.summary: A binary search tree avoids shifting but degenerates into a linked list and still costs one disk read per level.

chapters.name: PAGES AND FANOUT
chapters.summary: Packing a whole 8 KB page into each node gives a fanout near 500 and fits ten million rows in three levels.

chapters.name: B-TREE RULES
chapters.summary: Sorted keys, k+1 children, range boundaries, equal leaf depth and half-full nodes keep a B-tree balanced.

chapters.name: B-TREE SEARCH
chapters.summary: A lookup reads one node per level, and a B-tree can stop early when the key sits in an internal node.

chapters.name: B-TREE INSERT
chapters.summary: Inserts fill the target leaf and split full nodes upward, so the tree only grows at the root and stays balanced.

chapters.name: B-TREE VS B+TREE
chapters.summary: B+tree internal nodes are signposts and real entries live in linked leaves, giving wider nodes and cheap ranges.

chapters.name: B+TREE INSERT
chapters.summary: B+tree leaf splits copy the separator up and every key always stays in a leaf.

chapters.name: LOOKUP AND RANGE SCAN
chapters.summary: Point lookups follow the tree to a leaf, then range scans walk the leaf links instead of climbing back up.

chapters.name: B+TREE DELETE
chapters.summary: Deletes borrow from a sibling or merge thin leaves, rippling upward only when the root shrinks.

chapters.name: WHY B+TREE WINS
chapters.summary: Higher fanout, predictable lookups, linked-leaf range scans and dense full scans make the B+tree the default.

chapters.name: CLUSTERED VS SECONDARY
chapters.summary: A secondary index reaches the primary key first, so it needs a second walk unless the index covers the query.

chapters.name: COMPOSITE INDEXES
chapters.summary: An index on (a, b) serves a and a+b but not b alone: equality columns come first, range columns last.

chapters.name: THE COST OF INDEXES
chapters.summary: Every index adds write work and splits, and random keys leave pages partly empty, so index only what queries use.

chapters.name: EXPLAIN AND GOTCHAS
chapters.summary: EXPLAIN exposes the plan, and wrapped columns, leading wildcards, type mismatches, low selectivity or too many indexes hide an index.

chapters.name: RECAP
chapters.summary: Indexes turn linear scans into logarithmic lookups, but they cost writes and must be proven with EXPLAIN.
